section.title: Peace with God
section.sectionRationale: With justification by faith established through Abraham, Paul now unfolds its glorious results. Because we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God, access into grace, and a sure hope of glory. That hope holds even in suffering, for suffering produces perseverance, character, and hope, and hope does not disappoint because God has poured His love into our hearts by the Spirit. The ground of it all is the death of Christ for us while we were still sinners and enemies, and the passage soars on an argument from the greater to the lesser: if God reconciled us by His Son's death when we were enemies, how much more will He save us by His Son's life now that we are His friends.
section.thesis: Having been justified by faith, believers enjoy peace with God, standing in grace and rejoicing in hope, a hope unshaken even by suffering because God's love is poured into their hearts; for while we were still sinners and enemies Christ died for us, and having been reconciled by His death we shall surely be saved by His life.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the fruits of justification, peace, access, and rejoicing hope even in suffering; the proof of God's love in Christ dying for the ungodly; and the how much more assurance that those reconciled by His death will be saved by His life.

units.label: Peace, access, and rejoicing hope
units.note: the fruits of justification, even in suffering

verses.text: Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have {{eirene|peace}} with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,
through whom we have gained access by faith into this grace in which we stand. And we rejoice in the {{elpis|hope}} of the glory of God.
Not only that, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces perseverance;
And hope does not disappoint us, because God has poured out His {{agape|love}} into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, whom He has given us.

units.label: Christ died for the ungodly
units.note: God proves His love while we were still sinners

verses.text: For at just the right time, while we were still powerless, Christ died for the ungodly.
Very rarely will anyone die for a righteous man, though for a good man someone might possibly dare to die.
But God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

units.label: Reconciled, saved by His life
units.note: the how much more of assurance

verses.text: Therefore, since we have now been justified by His blood, how much more shall we be saved from wrath through Him!
For if, when we were enemies of God, we were {{katallasso|reconciled}} to Him through the death of His Son, how much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved through His life!
Not only that, but we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.

eirene.gloss: Peace, in the deep biblical sense of wholeness and restored relationship, echoing the Hebrew shalom. This is not merely a feeling of calm but an objective reality: the war between the sinner and God is over. Having been justified, believers have peace with God, no longer under condemnation but welcomed as friends through our Lord Jesus Christ.

elpis.gloss: Hope, confident expectation of the glory of God. Christian hope is not uncertain wishing but settled assurance grounded in what God has already done in Christ. It holds firm even in suffering and does not disappoint, because it rests not on circumstances but on the love of God poured into the heart by the Spirit.

agape.gloss: Love, the self-giving love of God. It is proved not in words but in the death of Christ for us while we were still sinners and enemies. This love is poured out into the hearts of believers by the Holy Spirit, giving inward assurance that matches the outward demonstration at the cross.

katallasso.gloss: To reconcile, to change from enmity to friendship, to bring parties who were at war into peace. God reconciled us to Himself through the death of His Son while we were still His enemies. Reconciliation is His work, received as a gift, and it is the relational side of justification: the barrier is removed and the relationship restored.

basic.context: Paul has proved that sinners are justified by faith, using Abraham. Now he draws out what justification actually brings. The word therefore ties it all to what came before: because we are declared righteous, we have peace with God, we stand in His grace, and we look forward with joy to sharing His glory. Then Paul shows that this hope holds even under suffering, and grounds the whole thing in the love of God shown at the cross.
basic.hermeneutics: Read this as a chain of results flowing from justification, marked by therefore, and by two how much more arguments. Paul reasons from the greater to the lesser: if God did the hardest thing, dying for us while we were enemies, He will surely do the easier thing, saving us now that we are His friends. The logic is meant to give believers rock-solid assurance.
basic.originalLanguages: The first fruit is eirene, peace with God, the end of the war between the sinner and his Maker. Believers rejoice in elpis, hope, that holds even in suffering. That hope rests on agape, the love of God poured into the heart by the Spirit and proved at the cross. And the relationship itself is restored through katallasso, reconciliation, God changing enemies into friends through the death of His Son.
basic.typology: The peace and access Paul describes fulfill what the temple system only pictured. Under the old covenant access to God was guarded and limited; now, through Christ, believers have gained access by faith into grace and stand there freely. The reconciliation of enemies to God completes what every sacrifice for sin was reaching toward.
basic.christ: Everything here comes through our Lord Jesus Christ. He is the one through whom we have peace, through whom we gained access, and whose death for the ungodly proves God's love. Justified by His blood and reconciled by His death, we are saved by His life, His risen, interceding life. Christ crucified and risen is the ground of both our peace and our assurance.
basic.god: God is the one who justifies, who pours His love into believers' hearts by the Spirit, and who proves His love at the cross. The passage shows a God who takes the initiative toward enemies, reconciling them to Himself at the cost of His own Son. His love is not a reward for the lovely but a gift lavished on sinners.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 8 develops the same assurance: nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ. Ephesians 2 says Christ is our peace, reconciling us to God through the cross. 2 Corinthians 5 declares that God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ. James 1 echoes that trials produce perseverance.
basic.oneStory: From Eden the human race has been at war with God. The whole Bible moves toward peace restored. Here Paul announces that in Christ the war is over: enemies are reconciled, sinners are justified, and a sure hope of glory is given. The love that God has been showing all along is proved at the cross and poured into our hearts, carrying us all the way to glory.

context.literary:
Romans 5:1-11 is one of the places where scholars disagree about where a paragraph belongs. Some attach it to chapters 1 to 4, as the close of the argument about justification. Others attach it to chapters 5 to 8, as the opening of a new section about life under grace. The truth may be that it is a hinge, and the vocabulary suggests why. The word 'justified' in verse 1 looks back, while 'peace,' 'hope,' 'love,' 'Spirit' and 'saved' look ahead, and all of them will be gathered up in chapter 8, which ends with the same confidence that nothing can separate us from the love of God.

The paragraph has a clear shape. Verses 1 and 2 state two present blessings, peace and access, and one future one, rejoicing in hope. Verses 3 to 5 expand the third by following a chain of steps from suffering to hope, ending with the love of God poured out. Verses 6 to 8 then give the ground of that love, the death of Christ, in three short lines that grow more astonishing: for the powerless, for the ungodly, for sinners. Verses 9 and 10 turn it into two arguments from the greater to the lesser, and verse 11 closes by returning to the verb that began the paragraph's third strand, 'rejoice.'

Notice the triple use of the Greek verb kauchaomai, 'boast' or 'exult,' in verses 2, 3 and 11. The word that Paul banished in 3:27 and 4:2 comes back, but now the object is changed. The believer's boasting is in hope, in sufferings and in God Himself. Everything Paul has taken from human pride he gives back as praise of God.
context.historical:
Paul wrote to people who lived in the shadow of the pax Romana, the peace the empire claimed to have secured by arms. Roman religion also thought in terms of the pax deorum, the favour of the gods, which had to be kept through sacrifice and ritual. To a hearer in Rome, a claim to have peace with the highest God as a settled possession through faith would sound extraordinary. It would also set the Christians' loyalty apart, since their peace did not depend on the emperor or on appeasing the gods.

The sufferings Paul mentions were real. Romans 8:35-36 lists tribulation, distress, persecution, famine and sword, and Romans 12:12 and 12:14 speak of patience in affliction and of blessing persecutors. The church in Rome would soon know the emperor's hostility, and even at the time of writing, being a Christian could mean strain with family and with the civic religious life of the city. Paul does not say suffering is good in itself. He says that those who are already at peace with God can face it with a different expectation.

The scene of verse 7 also has its own context. In the ancient world, dying for a good benefactor or a righteous friend was recognised as the highest sort of loyalty, and stories of such deaths were praised. Paul draws on that ideal to measure the cross against it. If a person might dare to die for someone good, verse 7, Christ died for those who were not even that, and the 'right time' of verse 6 is part of a larger plan in which God acted in the fullness of time, Galatians 4:4.
context.canonical:
The words that open the paragraph reach back to the Old Testament's greeting and blessing. The priestly blessing asks that the LORD lift up His face toward His people and give them peace, Numbers 6:26. The prophets promised that a work of righteousness would bring peace and quiet confidence, Isaiah 32:17, and announced peace to those far and near, Isaiah 57:19, a text Paul will quote when he writes to the Ephesians, Ephesians 2:17. Isaiah 53:5 says the punishment that brought us peace was laid on the Servant, which is the same cross Romans 5 sets out.

The theme of access is found in the tabernacle. Only the priests drew near, and only the high priest passed behind the veil. Hebrews 10:19-22 takes the language of this paragraph and says that believers have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus. First Peter 3:18 says Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, 'to bring you to God,' using the same family of words as Paul's 'access.'

The chain from suffering to hope appears in several places in the New Testament. James 1:2-4 speaks of the testing of faith that develops perseverance, and 1 Peter 1:6-7 says that trials prove the genuineness of faith like gold refined by fire. Paul himself returns to it in 2 Corinthians 4:17 and in Romans 8:18-25. The assurance of verses 9 and 10 is developed in Romans 8:31-39, where the logic of God not sparing His own Son is carried to its conclusion. And the language of reconciliation recurs in 2 Corinthians 5:18-21, Ephesians 2:13-18 and Colossians 1:21-22, three places where Paul states the doctrine in a different setting.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants believers to live as people who are sure of their footing. After four chapters in which sin, wrath and the law have dominated the discussion, he gives the other side of the account. A justified person is at peace, stands in grace and has a hope that cannot be put to shame. Paul writes so that his readers will not mistake justification for a legal fiction that leaves them anxious and exposed. The verdict has real effects: the war has ended, the door has opened, and the future has been settled.

He also means to prepare believers for suffering. The Roman Christians did not need to be told that life is hard. They needed a way to understand it. By linking suffering to hope in verses 3 to 5, Paul gives them a reason not to be crushed by it: because God's love has been poured out within them, the troubles of the present cannot undo what has been secured.

Paul has a theological purpose as well. He wants to show that the love of God is not an abstract idea but a concrete event, the death of Christ at a certain time for particular kinds of people. The cross is not only the ground of justification but the supreme demonstration of love, verse 8, and the believer's whole confidence rests on this single fact. If God has done the greater thing, He will certainly do the lesser.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage is almost entirely descriptive, and that is its power. Paul does not say 'try to have peace' or 'strive to hold on to hope.' He says we have peace, we stand in grace, God has poured out His love. Where there is a subjunctive in the textual tradition of verse 1, it is the only moment where the paragraph might seem to command, and even there the thing to be enjoyed already exists.

One application is that believers should let the facts set the tone of their lives. A person who is justified does not need to work his way into God's favour and so is freed from performance anxiety before God. Another is that suffering is to be met with a settled expectation, not with denial. Paul does not tell the sufferer to pretend, and he does not say that all suffering has a hidden purpose that can be named. He says that those who are in Christ will find that perseverance, character and hope are formed in them as they suffer. We should be careful not to turn the chain into a promise that every hardship will produce a stronger person automatically, since the passage states what happens within the life of the justified and under the Spirit's work.

A third application is how we speak about God's love. The description of verses 6 to 8 forbids talk of earning love by worthiness. It also forbids despair, because the love was shown when we were still sinners.

debates.question: Does Paul say 'we have peace' or 'let us have peace' in verse 1?

views.label: We have peace, the indicative
views.case: The two Greek forms, echomen with a short vowel or a long one, are almost identical in sound, and the manuscripts are divided. The BSB text reads 'we have' and notes 'let us have' as an alternative. The indicative suits the context. Everything around it is a statement of what justification has secured, and a command would sit oddly among so many descriptions. Verse 2's 'we have gained access' and verse 11's 'we have now received reconciliation' are of the same kind.

views.label: Let us have peace, the subjunctive
views.case: Some of the earliest and best manuscripts read the subjunctive, and the Greek 'let us' could be an exhortation to enjoy and to keep the peace in the face of trouble, as in the verses that follow. It might also be read as 'let us go on having,' a call to take hold of what has been given.

views.label: A hybrid understanding
views.case: Others hold that even the subjunctive presupposes the peace. A person cannot be told to keep what he does not have. On this reading the difference in meaning is smaller than it first seems.

debates.bearing: The doctrinal weight is the same either way, since peace is already given by justification. The indicative fits best with the flow of the argument, and it makes assurance depend on what God has done and not on the effort of the believer.

debates.question: In reconciliation, who is reconciled to whom?

views.label: Sinners are reconciled to God
views.case: Verse 10 calls us 'enemies of God' and says we were reconciled to Him. Second Corinthians 5:20 makes the call explicit: 'be reconciled to God.' On this reading the hostility is mainly on the human side, and God has acted in love to remove the barrier that sinners raised.

views.label: God and sinners are reconciled to each other
views.case: The Greek word for reconciliation describes a change in a relationship between two parties, and in verse 9 Paul speaks of being saved from wrath. The enmity runs in both directions: sinners are hostile to God, Colossians 1:21, and God's holy wrath rests on sin, Romans 1:18. The cross deals with both.

views.label: God is the one who reconciles, and He is not Himself changed
views.case: Another emphasis is that God never ceases to love. He takes the initiative and reconciles us to Himself, 2 Corinthians 5:18-19. So the change is in the sinners' relation, not in God's character.

debates.bearing: Verses 8 to 10 hold both truths. God loves us even while we are enemies, and the same cross that shows His love also turns away the wrath that the rest of Romans has described. Reconciliation is wholly His doing, from first to last.

study.originalLanguages:
Take the word translated 'peace,' eirene, in verse 1. In the Greek Old Testament it regularly translates the Hebrew shalom, which means far more than the absence of conflict. It means wholeness, health, and right relationships, as in the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:26. When Paul says we have eirene with God, he is saying that the relationship has been made whole, not that we have found calm feelings.

In verse 2 the word 'access' is prosagoge, from the verb prosago, 'to bring to.' That verb is used in the Greek Old Testament of bringing priests and offerings near to God, and 1 Peter 3:18 uses it of Christ bringing us to God. It is also used in the sense of an introduction into the presence of a king. The related image is that someone has opened the door and led us in. The verb for 'we stand,' hestekamen, is in the perfect tense, which means that we have taken our stand and remain standing. The posture is settled, not shaky.

The word 'rejoice' in verses 2, 3 and 11, kauchaomai, is the verb for boasting that Paul excluded in 3:27. Jeremiah 9:23-24 said let no one boast in wisdom, strength or riches but only in the knowledge of the LORD, and Paul's use echoes that. The believer boasts in hope, in trial and in God.

In verses 3 and 4 the chain runs thlipsis, hypomone, dokime, elpis. Thlipsis is pressure or affliction, literally a crushing. Hypomone, usually 'perseverance' or 'endurance,' is built from the verbs for 'remain' and 'under,' and it describes staying put beneath a load. Dokime is the quality of having been tested and passed, the word used for metal proved in the fire, as in 1 Peter 1:7, and 'character' captures the sense of approved quality. Elpis, hope, is not wishful thinking but confident expectation.

Verse 5 says hope does not 'disappoint,' ou kataischynei, literally does not put to shame. It is the language of Psalm 25:3, where none who wait on the LORD will be put to shame. The love of God has been 'poured out,' ekkechytai, a perfect passive verb, which pictures a flood that has been released and still stands in the heart. The verb of pouring is the one the prophets use for the outpouring of the Spirit, Joel 2:28, and Titus 3:6 says He was poured out abundantly.

In verses 6 to 10 Paul uses four words for what we were: powerless, ungodly, sinners, enemies. Each is more severe, and the preposition hyper, 'on behalf of,' appears in each of the first three statements of Christ's death. In verse 8 'proves' is synistesin, a present tense verb meaning to commend or demonstrate, so that God is continually showing His love in the cross.

The word for reconciliation, katallasso, comes from allasso, 'to change,' and in Greek of the period it described the change of relationship between two parties, such as husband and wife, as in 1 Corinthians 7:11. In Paul's letters the word is used of God and humanity in only a few places, and in each the initiative is God's. Finally, 'how much more,' pollo mallon in verses 9 and 10, is the standard form of argument from the greater to the lesser, and 'saved from wrath' uses the article, 'the wrath,' the same term Paul has used since 1:18.

typology.fulfillment: The tabernacle kept sinners at a distance. The high priest alone passed the veil, once a year, with blood, Leviticus 16:2-3. Paul's word for access, prosagoge, is the vocabulary of being brought near. In Christ the veil is opened, Hebrews 10:19-20, so that all believers have confidence to draw near. The type falls short because the high priest entered and left, and the people stood outside, while believers stand permanently in the grace into which they have been brought.

The fellowship or peace offering, in Hebrew a word from the same root as shalom, was a meal eaten in the presence of the LORD after blood had been shed, Leviticus 7:11-15. It pictured peace with God as a shared table. In Christ the table has become permanent, since He is the one who made peace by His blood, Colossians 1:20, and who will eat with His people forever, Revelation 3:20. The type falls short in that the offerer brought the animal himself and had to bring it again, while the peace of verse 1 is a gift provided by God.

Israel's forty years were a time of humbling and testing so that God might know what was in their hearts and teach them to live by every word from His mouth, Deuteronomy 8:2-5. Paul sees in the experience of the justified a similar pattern of trial that leads to proven character and hope. In Christ the pattern is fulfilled since He passed the test Israel failed, Matthew 4:1-4, and now His people are sustained in theirs by the Spirit. The type falls short because Israel's testing often ended in failure, while the believer's endurance is the fruit of God's love poured out within.

typology.type: Hiding in the garden and walking with God
typology.fulfillment: After the fall the man and woman hid from God among the trees, Genesis 3:8. Their fear of His presence is the first evidence of enmity. Romans 5 reverses it: believers 'rejoice in God' and stand in His grace. The Spirit, whom they have been given, brings them into the presence from which Adam fled. The type falls short in that Adam's hiding was only a shadow of enmity, while the enmity Paul describes runs deeper than hiding.

study.christ:
Every blessing in the paragraph is said to come 'through our Lord Jesus Christ,' verses 1, 2, 11, and the phrase is no formula. It is the place where the paragraph's logic turns. Peace is not a mood we find when circumstances improve, but a relationship opened by someone. Access is not a right we hold in ourselves but an entrance made by a person. Christ is the mediator in whom God and sinners are joined, and Ephesians 2:14 says it more briefly than Paul does here: 'He Himself is our peace.'

Next, Christ is presented through a precise historical event. Verse 6 says He died 'at just the right time,' and the gospels show how true this is. His death was not a mishap in a movement that lost its way, but the point toward which God had been working, Galatians 4:4. In verse 8 Paul adds that Christ died for us while we were still sinners, and so the time of His death was not after we had cleaned ourselves up. It was in the middle of our hostility. The love of God is not only declared in Christ but displayed in a single day.

Third, verse 7 sets up a comparison that exposes the depth of the cross. Paul says that very rarely will anyone die for a righteous man, though for a good man someone might possibly dare. He names no case. Then he says Christ died for people who had no claim of that kind. The cross is thus not merely generous but of an entirely different order. John 15:13 says there is no greater love than to lay down one's life for one's friends, and Romans 5 shows that Jesus laid His down for enemies.

Fourth, the two 'how much more' arguments show that Christ is both the payment and the guarantee. In verse 9 He is the one by whose blood we have been justified, and in verse 10 He is the one whose risen life saves us. It would be a mistake to read 'saved by His life' as though His death were not enough, since the point is that the death which reconciled enemies is joined to a life that never ends. Hebrews 7:25 says He always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through Him, and Romans 8:34 says He is at the right hand of God interceding for us.

Last, verse 11 shows that Christ's work has a goal beyond our relief. We rejoice 'in God' through Him. The cross does not only remove danger but opens enjoyment. The Son whose death made peace has also made it possible for us to take pleasure in the Father. The one who stood between God and sinners as the object of wrath now stands between them as the way to delight.

The text has no need of allegory. The relevant links are drawn by the New Testament itself: the peace made by blood in Colossians 1:20, the access through the veil in Hebrews 10, and the exchange of the righteous for the unrighteous in 1 Peter 3:18.
study.god:
This paragraph is one of the clearest windows in Scripture onto the character of God. The central fact is verse 8, where Paul says God 'proves His love for us.' The Greek verb is present tense, and the proof is not an argument or a feeling but a historical event. God does not demonstrate His love by words alone. He sent His Son. First John 4:10 says the same thing in other terms: love consists not in our loving God but in His loving us and sending His Son as the atoning sacrifice.

The paragraph shows that God's love comes first. We were powerless, ungodly, sinners, enemies, and nothing in the list attracts. Many pictures of the divine in the ancient world imagined gods who responded to the worthy. Paul shows a God whose love is the cause of everything else, not an answer to anything in us. That is a defining mark of grace, and it makes the doctrine of God in Romans very different from the religion of Rome.

God is also shown as holy, since the text assumes wrath and a need to be saved from it, verse 9. His love is not a soft indulgence that ignores sin. It is the love of a God who takes sin seriously enough to deal with it at the cost of His Son. The two attributes, holiness and love, are not rivals in this paragraph. The cross is where they are held together, and the believer's peace is built on both.

The paragraph is also trinitarian in its shape. The Father proves His love, the Son dies and lives, and the Holy Spirit pours the love of God into the heart, verse 5. Paul does not give a lecture on the Trinity, but the three act in a single saving movement, and the believer's assurance has all three behind it. The Spirit makes the objective love of the cross a subjective reality in the heart, and Romans 8:15-16 says the same Spirit testifies with our spirit that we are God's children.

Another attribute on display is God's faithfulness. The hope that does not disappoint rests on the fact that God has already done the hardest thing. Romans 8:32 draws the same inference: He who did not spare His own Son will freely give us all things. God's commitments are not tentative. What He began in justification He carries through to salvation, and the chain of verses 3 to 5 is the first stage of that.

For worship, the paragraph invites a particular kind of joy. Verse 11 says we rejoice in God. That means more than gratitude for gifts, since the gifts are not the end. The God who has made peace is Himself the treasure. Prayer, then, can begin from welcome and not from fear, since the Father who proved His love at the cross does not turn away those who come to Him through the Son.

crossReferences.note: The conclusion of the argument that Romans 5 begins. If God did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all, He will not fail to give us everything else. It repeats the logic of the how much more in verses 9 and 10, and moves from peace to the certainty of final glory.

Christ Himself is our peace, who tore down the dividing wall and reconciled both Jew and Gentile to God in one body through the cross. The passage ends with 'access to the Father by one Spirit,' which shows that Paul's word for access in Romans 5:2 is part of a larger teaching about the Trinity and the church.

God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, not counting men's trespasses against them. The phrase links the doctrine of reconciliation to the earlier language of crediting in Romans 4, and it shows that reconciliation is a work of God from beginning to end, with a message committed to His people.

Once alienated and hostile in mind, believers are now reconciled by Christ's physical body through death. Where Romans 5:10 calls us enemies, this verse shows the inner side of the enmity, which lay in the mind and in evil deeds, and adds that the goal is to be presented holy and blameless.

Believers have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, through the new and living way opened by His body. It gives the temple background of Paul's word for access and shows what stands behind the call to draw near in full assurance.

The testing of faith produces perseverance, and perseverance must finish its work for maturity. It runs parallel to Paul's chain in verses 3 and 4, though it goes on to call for joy in trials, and it shows that the idea was shared across the early church.

Trials prove the genuineness of faith like gold refined by fire, and result in praise and honour at the revelation of Jesus Christ. It gives the picture behind Paul's word for proven character, and ties the fruit of suffering to the final day.

The punishment that brought us peace was upon the Servant. Isaiah's words give the Old Testament root of the peace in Romans 5:1, showing that peace came by a substitute bearing the penalty, and that it was announced centuries before the cross.

The priestly blessing asks the LORD to lift up His face and give His people peace. It shows what the peace of Romans 5:1 means in its Old Testament setting: not an inward calm but the favour of God turned toward His people, which Christ now secures for all who believe.

Love consists not in our love for God but in His sending of His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins. It gives the same reading as verse 8, that the cross is the definition of love, and shows how the first letter of John repeats Paul's teaching in simpler words.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a man and woman who walked with God and ends with a multitude who see His face, and the long middle is the story of how the distance was crossed. In Genesis 3 the pair hid from God and were sent out of the garden. Cain went out from the presence of the LORD, Genesis 4:16. Babel's builders tried to make their own way up. The tabernacle and temple offered a narrow, mediated, repeated access, with a veil and guards, and Israel itself went into exile away from the land and the house. Throughout, the human problem is not only guilt but distance.

Romans 5:1-11 is the place where the distance is closed in the present. Paul says that we have peace, that we have gained access, and that we stand. He does not say we shall have peace one day. The reconciliation that Isaiah had foreseen, peace to the far and the near, has arrived, and the God who walked in the garden has made it possible for sinners to walk with Him again. The love of God, long visible in covenant and rescue, is now seen in its fullest form in a death for enemies.

The paragraph also sets up what follows. Because peace has come, Paul can go on to show how sin and death entered by one man and are overcome by another, Romans 5:12-21, and then how the Spirit makes God's people live in the freedom of sons, Romans 8. The assurance of verses 9 and 10 is the first of the steps that lead to the great chain of Romans 8:29-30, where those whom God justified He also glorified.

The story ends in the place that Paul's paragraph names as the goal of hope, the glory of God. In Revelation 21:3-4 the dwelling of God is with man and He wipes away every tear, and in Revelation 22:4 His servants see His face. What the paragraph calls access becomes sight, what it calls hope becomes possession, and the peace made at the cross becomes the peace of a world in which nothing stands between the Creator and His people.

quiz.q: What is the first result of being justified by faith, according to verse 1?

options.text: We have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.
options.note: Justification ends the enmity; the war between the sinner and God is over.

options.text: We are given a peaceful, calm feeling inside.
options.note: Inner peace may follow, but the point is objective peace with God, a restored relationship.

options.text: We are freed from all suffering in this life.
options.note: Paul says we still suffer, yet rejoice; peace with God is not the removal of hardship.

options.text: We earn a right standing by keeping the peace.
options.note: Peace is the fruit of justification by faith, not something we earn.

quiz.q: Why can believers rejoice even in their sufferings?

options.text: Because suffering produces perseverance, character, and hope that does not disappoint.
options.note: God uses suffering to forge a hope grounded in His love poured into our hearts.

options.text: Because suffering earns them extra merit before God.
options.note: Suffering forms character; it does not earn merit or acceptance.

options.text: Because they should pretend that pain does not hurt.
options.note: Paul is not denying the pain but pointing to what God works through it.

options.text: Because suffering guarantees an easier life to come.
options.note: Suffering does look toward a future hope, but the fruit is perseverance, character, and hope, not the promise of an easy life.

quiz.q: How does God prove His love for us, according to verse 8?

options.text: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
options.note: God's love is demonstrated at the cross, given to the undeserving.

options.text: By waiting until we had made ourselves worthy.
options.note: Christ died while we were still sinners, powerless, and ungodly.

options.text: By rewarding those who first loved Him.
options.note: The love is one-way grace toward enemies, not a reward for our love.

options.text: Mainly by giving us comfortable lives.
options.note: God is good to us, but the proof of His love is the death of Christ, not favorable circumstances.

quiz.q: What is the how much more argument in verses 9 and 10?

options.text: If God reconciled us by His Son's death when we were enemies, He will surely save us by His life.
options.note: Paul reasons from the harder act to the easier, grounding assurance.

options.text: If we try harder, God will love us even more.
options.note: The argument rests on Christ's finished work, not our effort.

options.text: That salvation is now uncertain and depends on us.
options.note: The point is the opposite: our salvation is made certain by Christ.

options.text: That reconciliation matters more than final salvation.
options.note: Both are precious, but Paul's point is that they belong together: reconciliation guarantees final salvation.

quiz.q: What does it mean that we have received reconciliation?

options.text: God has changed us from enemies into friends through the death of His Son.
options.note: Reconciliation is God's work, received as a gift, ending the enmity.

options.text: We have reconciled ourselves to God by our repentance.
options.note: Repentance is real, but reconciliation is accomplished by God through Christ's death and then received.

options.text: God and humanity met each other halfway.
options.note: God took the whole initiative toward enemies; it was not a mutual bargain.

options.text: It refers only to peace between people, not with God.
options.note: Paul speaks of being reconciled to God Himself through His Son.

questions: Paul says the justified have peace with God, a settled end to the war. How would living in the certainty of that peace, rather than fearing God's rejection, change your daily walk with Him?
Believers rejoice in the hope of glory even in suffering. Where is God using a present hardship to produce perseverance, character, and hope in you?
God proves His love in that Christ died for us while we were still sinners. How does knowing His love was given to you as an enemy, not a reward for your goodness, move your heart?
The Spirit pours God's love into our hearts. How have you known that inward assurance of being loved, and how might you ask God for a deeper sense of it?
If we were reconciled by Christ's death, how much more shall we be saved by His life. How does this how much more logic steady your assurance when you doubt your salvation?

translationNotes.note: The BSB footnote records a variant, let us have peace, reflecting strong manuscript support for the subjunctive. The BSB text reads we have peace, taking it as a statement of fact about the standing justification secures; either way the peace is a gift already given.
Rejoice renders a verb the BSB footnote notes can also be exult, used again in verses 3 and 11. It expresses confident, glad boasting in what God has done, not in ourselves.

Reconciled renders katallasso, to change from enmity to friendship. The verse stresses that reconciliation was accomplished through the death of God's Son while we were enemies, so that final salvation through His risen life is assured.
